title: The Blue Coupe
style: Narrate as a young man looking back on his life, in a calm, warm, intimate, cinematic tone. Slow pace. Leave a natural pause between sentences. Do not rush.

segments.text: Every city has one window you can't stop looking at. Mine was on Fifth Street. And behind the glass, under the lights, sat a blue coupe I could never afford.
I was nine when I first saw it. A poster, taped above my bed, corners curling from the damp. My dad said dreams like that were for other people. I believed him. For a while.
At nineteen, I washed bowls in a ramen shop until two in the morning. Six nights a week. Every tip went into a jar. Every coin had a job. Every coin was a piece of that car.

My first car cost less than a phone. It leaked, it rattled, and it died on me in the middle of a storm, three miles from home. So I pushed it. The whole way. Soaked to the bone. Laughing, because what else could I do?
I asked the bank for help, once. The man barely looked up. Declined. No history. No savings. No chance. I walked back out into the rain feeling about two inches tall.
So I stopped asking. Extra shifts. Weekend deliveries. I sold my games. My guitar. Summer turned to winter, and winter turned to rain again. My friends went out. I stayed in, and counted.
Then one night, I walked past the window, and it was gone. Just a little red sign. Sold. Someone else was driving my dream. I stood there for a long time. I almost quit. I really did.

A week later, an old mechanic named Ito called me. He'd found one. Same model. Same blue. Tired, rusted, forgotten in a barn. It needs work, he said. So do you. We rebuilt it together. Every night, for eight months.
And then, one morning, the rain finally stopped. I turned the key, and the engine woke up like it had been waiting for me too. I drove down Fifth Street. Past the window. And I didn't even slow down.
People ask me if it was worth it. The car is just metal. But the guy who built it? He's the one I was really chasing. Whatever your blue coupe is. Keep going.
